title: A new name, an old warning: Thursday the ECB showed its hand

pages.title: One name, one account: the ECB picks a successor and publishes its doubts

one-name-one-account-the-ecb-picks-a-pre.title: One name, one account: the ECB picks a successor and publishes its doubts
one-name-one-account-the-ecb-picks-a-pre.dek: Eurozone leaders backed Pablo Hernández de Cos for the top job on the same day Frankfurt released the minutes of its October pause. The name made the headlines. The account says more about your mortgage.
one-name-one-account-the-ecb-picks-a-pre.text: Two things came out of the euro’s institutions on Thursday. In Brussels, a majority of eurozone governments backed Pablo Hernández de Cos, 55, head of the Bank for International Settlements and governor of the Bank of Spain from 2018 to 2024, to succeed Christine Lagarde; he secured more support than the former Dutch governor Klaas Knot [1]. Lagarde leaves on 7 February 2027. France’s Laurence Boone is in line to take over market operations from Isabel Schnabel, and Germany’s Markus Brunnermeier to replace chief economist Philip Lane [1]. The appointments are to be made in December, after consultation [1]. In Frankfurt, the ECB published the account of its 28–29 October meeting, when it kept the deposit rate at 2.50% [2]. It is drier reading and more useful. Oil and gas futures had moved above the adverse scenario of September’s staff projections; inflation fixings peaked at 4.5% for January 2027 [2]. Members agreed communication should convey ‘that another rate hike would likely be necessary unless the inflation outlook improved significantly’ [2]. The pause, they wrote, ‘did not reflect diminished concern’ [2]. Economists quoted by Euronews call Hernández de Cos slightly more dovish than Knot, but expect the change of leadership alone to alter little [1]. That is the right expectation. A central bank that works is a committee with minutes, not a person with a temperament. On Thursday you saw both, and the minutes were louder. This is reporting, not investment advice.

15-agreed-15-proposed-brussels-rejects-t.title: 15% agreed, 15% proposed: Brussels rejects the premise, not the number
15-agreed-15-proposed-brussels-rejects-t.dek: Washington's overcapacity tariffs would cap the EU at the rate already in last year's deal. The Commission objects anyway, and it is right to object to the method.
15-agreed-15-proposed-brussels-rejects-t.text: China, the EU and other partners pushed back on Thursday against the tariffs of up to 20% that Washington proposed after its Section 301 probe into excess capacity [1]. For the EU, South Korea and Taiwan, which have trade deals with the US, the duties would be broadly capped at 15% [1]. That is the same number the EU agreed last year. Trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič still rejected the decision and said Washington should respect that 15% [1]. Why object to a number you already accepted? Because the instrument matters. A deal is a contract with two signatures. A Section 301 finding is a unilateral verdict that can be revised by one side. ‘The EU and the US share a real concern about global overcapacity, much of it state-driven and concentrated in third countries. We regret the lack of joint action,’ said Commission spokesman Olof Gill [1]. The new levies would not stack on sector tariffs such as those on cars and steel, a senior US official said [1]. China’s commerce ministry called the probe an act of unilateralism [1]. The dull lesson: in trade, the paperwork is the policy.

0-04-kroner-a-share-the-jet-fuel-bill-re.title: 0.04 kroner a share: the jet-fuel bill reaches an airline
0-04-kroner-a-share-the-jet-fuel-bill-re.dek: Norse Atlantic grounded every flight and warned of bankruptcy. It is not the first carrier this autumn.
0-04-kroner-a-share-the-jet-fuel-bill-re.text: Norwegian long-haul carrier Norse Atlantic cancelled all of Thursday’s flights and said its board would file for bankruptcy unless short-term financing was secured urgently [1]. At 0.04 kroner a share it was worth about $9.7 million [1]. Euronews links the crisis to surging jet-fuel prices since the war in the Middle East [1]. Spain’s Plus Ultra stopped flying on Tuesday, and airBaltic filed for Chapter 11 in September [1]. A war far away arrives as a fuel invoice. Airlines with thin margins pay it first, and passengers with booked tickets find out at the gate.

unacceptable-brazil-gets-its-own-tariff-.title: 'Unacceptable': Brazil gets its own tariff file
unacceptable-brazil-gets-its-own-tariff-.dek: Washington proposed separate duties on Brazilian goods, aircraft included.
unacceptable-brazil-gets-its-own-tariff-.text: In a separate announcement, the US Trade Representative also proposed additional tariffs on goods from Brazil, including aircraft, over alleged inaction on US trade concerns, France 24 reported [1]. The Brazilian president’s office called the measures ‘unacceptable’ and said Brasília would ‘not yield to this type of threat’ [1]. Two files in one week: the overcapacity probe for 14 economies, and a single-country case for the 15th.

plus-2-08-without-new-york-the-dax-climb.title: Plus 2.08% without New York: the DAX climbs back over 25,000
plus-2-08-without-new-york-the-dax-climb.dek: Wall Street was shut for Thanksgiving. Frankfurt bought what had fallen most, on thin volume and a hint that US tariffs may be milder than feared.
plus-2-08-without-new-york-the-dax-climb.text: The DAX ended Thursday 2.08% higher at 25,215.52 points, back above 25,000 after Wednesday’s fall to its lowest level since July, dpa-AFX reported [4]. The rebound followed the turn that US technology shares made late on Wednesday [4]. ‘Nach den turbulenten Tagen bietet die Pause Anlegern eine willkommene Gelegenheit zum Durchatmen,’ wrote eToro analyst Maximilian Wienke: the holiday gives investors a chance to catch their breath [4]. New York was closed for Thanksgiving; trading thinned out through the afternoon without spoiling the mood, as Andreas Lipkow wrote for wallstreet:online [2]. The buying went to what had been sold hardest: chipmaker Infineon and Siemens Energy, plus carmakers still lifted by Wednesday’s analyst notes [2]. Handelsblatt reported signs that the planned US tariffs on EU goods could turn out milder than feared [3]. Chief analyst Jochen Stanzl put it plainly: on Monday investors bought because of Jensen Huang’s return, ‘jetzt wegen des Preises’, now because of the price [3]. Across Europe the rise was broad: by Boursorama’s figures after the cash close, Milan was up 2.36%, Madrid 2.26%, the Euro Stoxx 50 2.11%, London 1.75%, Paris 1.61% and Zurich 1.04% [1]. One good day after a bad one restores the level, not the argument. The question Stanzl raised, whether the AI billions pay off when rates rise, is still open [3]. This is reporting, not investment advice.

autos-plus-3-18-food-plus-0-05-the-shape.title: Autos plus 3.18%, food plus 0.05%: the shape of a rebound
autos-plus-3-18-food-plus-0-05-the-shape.dek: The sectors that fell hardest rose most. The safe ones barely moved.
autos-plus-3-18-food-plus-0-05-the-shape.text: Among the Euro Stoxx sector indexes, autos and parts rose 3.18%, technology 3.06%, basic resources 3.00% and banks 2.49% on Thursday, Boursorama’s figures after the close show [1]. Food and beverages gained 0.05% [1]. Andreas Lipkow wrote that investors focused on the tech and car shares that had come under heavy pressure recently [2]. A rebound led by the most-sold sectors is a relief rally, not yet a change of view. The quiet number is food’s 0.05%: nobody needed to buy the shelter back, because nobody had run from it. This is reporting, not investment advice.

taiex-plus-2-50-shenzhen-minus-3-45-asia.title: Taiex plus 2.50%, Shenzhen minus 3.45%: Asia did not agree
taiex-plus-2-50-shenzhen-minus-3-45-asia.dek: Before Europe opened, Asia's markets split down the middle.
taiex-plus-2-50-shenzhen-minus-3-45-asia.text: Boursorama’s closing levels show an Asia that read Wednesday’s late Wall Street rebound in different ways [1]. Taiwan’s Taiex gained 2.50% to 39,151.81, Hong Kong’s Hang Seng 1.19% and Tokyo’s Nikkei 225 0.86% [1]. The Shanghai Composite was flat, up 0.01%, while the Shenzhen Composite fell 3.45% [1]. One region, one night, three verdicts. That is what a market is supposed to look like. This is reporting, not investment advice.

podium-vs-print-light-years-away-and-1-6.title: Podium vs Print: "light years away", and €1.6 trillion
podium-vs-print-light-years-away-and-1-6.dek: EU leaders spent Thursday describing how far apart they are on the 2028–2034 budget. The documents on the table say exactly how far.
podium-vs-print-light-years-away-and-1-6.text: The podium. ‘We are light years away from a solution to this problem,’ Giorgia Meloni said in Brussels on Thursday [1]. Hungary’s Péter Magyar put the chance of a deal at the summit at ‘pretty much zero’ and said a Christmas deal ‘doesn’t seem likely either’ [1]. European Parliament president Roberta Metsola said MEPs would not rubber-stamp a deal [2]. The print. António Costa’s draft is a seven-year budget of almost €1.6 trillion [1]. Seven ‘frugals’ — Austria, Belgium, Germany, Denmark, Finland, the Netherlands and Sweden — want it trimmed; 17 ‘Friends of Cohesion’ reject further cuts [1]. Beside it sits the Commission’s €45 billion loan for Ukraine, financed through joint debt, from which three countries want to opt out [1]. Friedrich Merz warned Germany could block the budget if countries pulled out of supporting Ukraine [1]. The gap. The speeches describe a chasm. The papers describe a negotiation over a number with a known size and two clear camps. Costa broke the summit into small groups, starting with the frugals [1]. That is what closing a gap looks like: dull, in rooms, line by line.

16-8-billion-for-the-interior-the-budget.title: €16.8 billion for the interior: the budget votes start to land
16-8-billion-for-the-interior-the-budget.dek: The Bundestag passed the interior ministry's 2027 budget, about €1 billion more than this year. The final vote is on Friday.
16-8-billion-for-the-interior-the-budget.text: The Bundestag approved the interior ministry’s budget for 2027 on Thursday, BR24 reported, about one billion euros more than this year [2]. Presseonline put the total at €16.8 billion, with more for the federal police, the Federal Criminal Police Office and the domestic intelligence service [1]. Minister Alexander Dobrindt said the budget repositions Germany on security, with reforms of the intelligence service, the federal police and cyber defence [2]. The justice, economy, housing, agriculture and family budgets followed during the day; the whole federal budget is due for its final vote on Friday [1].

27-december-serbia-sets-a-date-to-choose.title: 27 December: Serbia sets a date to choose Vučić's successor
27-december-serbia-sets-a-date-to-choose.dek: A presidential election two days after Christmas.
27-december-serbia-sets-a-date-to-choose.text: Serbia will hold a presidential election on 27 December to choose Aleksandar Vučić’s successor, The Guardian’s Europe live blog reported on Thursday [1]. An election date is the most ordinary institutional fact there is. It is also the one that matters most.

the-annex-3-6-million-children-7-595-exp.title: The Annex: 3.6 million children, 7,595 exposed, and no added risk
the-annex-3-6-million-children-7-595-exp.dek: A Scandinavian register study finds no higher risk of autism, ADHD or learning disorders in children whose mothers took ADHD medicine in pregnancy. Its value is in the size of the denominator.
the-annex-3-6-million-children-7-595-exp.text: Many women with ADHD stop their medication when they become pregnant, for lack of evidence, and that can hurt their mental health and family stability, BMJ Group notes [1]. A study published in The BMJ on Wednesday adds the evidence. Researchers used health registers in Denmark, Norway and Sweden covering 3,643,376 children born between 2000 and 2021, followed for a median of nine to ten years [1]. Of these, 7,595 (0.2%) were exposed to ADHD medication in pregnancy [1]. After adjusting for factors such as the mother’s age, education, smoking and her own ADHD diagnosis, neither exposure overall nor by drug type — methylphenidate in 69% of cases, amphetamines 20%, atomoxetine 7% — was linked to a higher risk of any neurodevelopmental disorder [1]. The authors write that concerns about such risks ‘do not justify discontinuation of ADHD medication in pregnancy’ [1]. The limits are stated too: the study is observational, and unmeasured factors such as ADHD severity or genetics could play a part [1]. That honesty is the point of the Annex. A good study tells you what it found and what it cannot rule out, and lets the doctor and the patient decide. This is reporting, not medical advice.

misinformation-prevails-in-an-informatio.title: 'Misinformation prevails in an information vacuum': the pantry panic
misinformation-prevails-in-an-informatio.dek: Sensible government advice to keep three days of supplies has been turned into doomsday rumours online.
misinformation-prevails-in-an-informatio.text: Countries such as the UK and Japan have advised households to keep at least three days of essentials, and online rumours have turned that guidance into talk of an impending world war, Euronews and AFP report [1]. UK media reported that tinned-food sales at Iceland briefly rose 40% in late October [1]. ‘Misinformation prevails in an information vacuum,’ said Yotam Ophir of the University at Buffalo: when advice lacks context, people ‘fill the gap with their own alternative explanations’ [1]. The calm answer is more detail, not less advice. A three-day shelf is a plan, not a prophecy.

absurd-amodei-on-free-will-and-the-machi.title: 'Absurd': Amodei on free will and the machines
absurd-amodei-on-free-will-and-the-machi.dek: Anthropic's chief rejects the claim that humans should hand decisions to AI.
absurd-amodei-on-free-will-and-the-machi.text: ‘No, I do not believe that we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems, and it’s absurd to suggest that I do,’ Anthropic’s Dario Amodei wrote on Wednesday, after an Axios report [1]. ‘We should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security,’ he added [1]. Euronews notes he had earlier said that in ‘life-critical, safety-critical cases, we really want to turn it over’ [1]. The useful test of such words is not the post. It is which decisions the products actually take away from you.

301-82-for-friday-the-cold-week-gets-a-l.title: €301.82 for Friday: the cold week gets a little dearer
301-82-for-friday-the-cold-week-gets-a-l.dek: German wholesale power for Friday averages above €300 a megawatt hour, the most since 11 November. Brent, meanwhile, rose on mines in Hormuz. Only one of the two arrives on your meter.
301-82-for-friday-the-cold-week-gets-a-l.text: Friday’s day-ahead auction for Germany and Luxembourg averages €301.82 per megawatt hour, up from €291.77 for Thursday, according to Energy-Charts data from Bundesnetzagentur and SMARD [1]. Friday’s quarter-hours range from €203.35 at 23:45 to €426.32 at 08:15 [1]. It is the highest daily average since 11 November. The cause is unremarkable: high pressure and cold air over much of Germany, with light to moderate frost and persistent frost in the east and south on Friday, the German weather service reported [3]. Oil moved for other reasons. Brent was up $1.64, or 1.73%, at $96.25 a barrel on Thursday afternoon after Iran said mines struck two tankers in the Strait of Hormuz and the Houthis claimed an attack on Ras Tanura [2]. PVM’s Tamas Varga sees a new range of around $88–97 for Brent [2]. WTI will have no settlement because of Thanksgiving [2]. The power price has a meteorological explanation; the oil price, for now, has a rumour and a range. This is reporting, not investment advice.

88-to-97-dollars-an-analyst-s-range-for-.title: $88 to $97: an analyst's range for a nervous barrel
88-to-97-dollars-an-analyst-s-range-for-.dek: Mines in Hormuz pushed Brent up again. A supply surplus and higher rates may cap it.
88-to-97-dollars-an-analyst-s-range-for-.text: Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said two tankers exploded and caught fire after hitting sea mines north of Oman’s Khasab port; one was a supertanker carrying more than two million barrels, according to the Guards [1]. Brent rose to $96.25 [1]. PVM’s Tamas Varga said a perceived supply surplus and sticky inflation, which forces central banks to raise rates, could ‘set a ceiling’ on prices [1]. OPEC+ ministers meet on 29 November and may roll over current targets for the first quarter of 2027, two sources told Reuters [1]. This is reporting, not investment advice.

a-refinery-a-pipeline-station-a-power-pl.title: A refinery, a pipeline station, a power plant: the energy front
a-refinery-a-pipeline-station-a-power-pl.dek: Ukraine's overnight drones went for Russia's oil machinery again.
a-refinery-a-pipeline-station-a-power-pl.text: A new fire broke out at the Kuibyshev refinery in Samara on Thursday morning, a day after it was struck, and Ukrainian forces hit the Subkhankulovo station, a hub of the Transneft trunk pipeline system in Bashkortostan [1]. A drone attack also caused a fire with serious damage at the Slavyansk ECO refinery in Krasnodar region, Reuters reported [2]. Pipelines and refineries are the war’s quiet targets: each one changes what Russia can sell abroad.

boone-and-brunnermeier-the-two-names-und.title: Boone and Brunnermeier: the two names under the headline
boone-and-brunnermeier-the-two-names-und.dek: The ECB's markets desk and its chief economist are changing hands too, which matters as much as the president.
boone-and-brunnermeier-the-two-names-und.text: Besides the presidency, eurozone governments discussed two Executive Board seats on Thursday, Euronews reported [1]. France’s Laurence Boone is expected to take responsibility for market operations from Isabel Schnabel, who leaves on 3 January 2027 for the IMF [1]. Germany’s Markus Brunnermeier is in line to replace chief economist Philip Lane, whose term ends on 31 May 2027 [1]. In October it was Lane who proposed keeping rates unchanged [2]. A president chairs the committee. The chief economist writes the first draft of its thinking.

4-5-for-january-what-the-markets-priced-.title: 4.5% for January: what the markets priced into the pause
4-5-for-january-what-the-markets-priced-.dek: The ECB's account records an inflation fixing that peaks early next year.
4-5-for-january-what-the-markets-priced-.text: In Isabel Schnabel’s market briefing to the October meeting, inflation fixings for 2026 and 2027 had shifted higher, peaking at 4.5% for January 2027 and staying above 2.5% until the first quarter of 2028, the account shows [1]. Market pricing pointed to a deposit-rate peak around 3% [1]. Diesel crack spreads stood above their levels after Russia’s 2022 invasion [1]. The account is a list of prices the committee looked at. That is why it is worth reading.

ordinary-ledger-minus-30-2-600-shops-and.title: Ordinary Ledger: minus 30.2, 600 shops, and a 14-day return
ordinary-ledger-minus-30-2-600-shops-and.dek: German consumer mood barely moved before Christmas, a British discounter went under, and an online marketplace promised to make refunds simpler. Three entries from the shop floor.
ordinary-ledger-minus-30-2-600-shops-and.text: −30.2. The NIM consumer climate, powered by GfK, rose 0.7 points to −30.2 for December, from a revised −30.9 [1]. Income expectations rose 1.8 points to −13.9, but are almost 14 points lower than a year ago; the propensity to buy edged up to −11.5 [1]. ‘Für das bevorstehende Weihnachtsgeschäft sind das keine guten Vorzeichen,’ said NIM’s Rolf Bürkl: not good signs for Christmas trade [1]. Price expectations rose to 2.8, despite the fuel rebate [1]. 600 shops. UK discounter Poundland went into administration on Wednesday, putting about 11,000 jobs and 600 stores at risk [2]. Its owner said that even after £100 million of cost savings the business remained ‘vulnerable to inflationary pressures’ [2]. The shops keep trading for now [2]. 14 days. Temu committed to EU consumer authorities to make withdrawals, returns and refunds simpler, to show prices more clearly and to drop messages pressing shoppers to buy, the Commission said [3]. National authorities will monitor compliance [3]. On the eve of Black Friday, that is the useful entry: a right you can use, not a discount you are told to chase.

buy-what-you-eat-use-the-oldest-first-a-.title: Buy what you eat, use the oldest first: a sensible pantry
buy-what-you-eat-use-the-oldest-first-a-.dek: Germany's civil protection office has advice for emergency supplies that avoids waste.
buy-what-you-eat-use-the-oldest-first-a-.text: Germany’s Federal Office of Civil Protection and Disaster Assistance recommends buying food that people regularly eat and using up older supplies first, and storing non-perishables airtight in a cool, dry, dark place, Euronews reports [1]. The UK’s Be Ready campaign suggests building up supplies over several shopping trips and checking expiry dates every six months [1]. In the EU, more than half of the nearly 58 million tonnes of food waste in 2024 came from households [1]. A reserve you rotate is preparedness. A reserve you forget is waste.

15-6-the-saving-instinct-eases-for-a-sec.title: 15.6: the saving instinct eases for a second month
15-6-the-saving-instinct-eases-for-a-sec.dek: Germans want to save a little less. Their economic outlook dimmed for the first time in seven months.
15-6-the-saving-instinct-eases-for-a-sec.text: The NIM saving indicator fell 1.6 points to 15.6, its second decline in a row, which helped lift the consumer climate slightly [1]. Economic expectations, after six increases, fell 3.7 points to −1.6 [1]. The survey ran from 28 October to 9 November with about 2,000 interviews [1]. Households saving a little less while expecting a little worse is not a contradiction. It is what happens when prices have already eaten the cushion.

refunds-reviews-and-no-forced-games-temu.title: Refunds, reviews and no forced games: Temu signs the dull rules
refunds-reviews-and-no-forced-games-temu.dek: After a €200 million fine in May and critical findings in November, the marketplace promised EU consumer authorities a list of ordinary obligations. That is what enforcement is for.
refunds-reviews-and-no-forced-games-temu.text: Temu has committed to change several practices to comply with EU consumer law, the Commission said on Thursday [1]. The list is unglamorous: more accessible company information, better customer support, simpler withdrawals, returns and refunds, more reliable reviews, clearer pricing, an end to messages pressing customers to buy, removal of forced gamification features, substantiated environmental claims and a clearer checkout [1]. ‘Temu’s commitments are an important step towards ensuring consumers can shop online with confidence,’ said commissioner Michael McGrath, adding that the Commission would ‘continue to closely monitor’ compliance [1]. In May the Commission fined Temu €200 million after investigators found dangerous baby toys and faulty chargers on the platform; in early November preliminary findings said it had not changed enough [1]. The case now passes to national authorities [1]. That is the right order of things. Regulation rarely wins with one dramatic fine. It wins when a company’s lawyers conclude that obeying the boring rules is cheaper than arguing about them.

jetzt-wegen-des-preises-buying-chips-on-.title: 'Jetzt wegen des Preises': buying chips on price, not faith
jetzt-wegen-des-preises-buying-chips-on-.dek: Infineon and Siemens Energy led Frankfurt's rebound. The AI question underneath is unchanged.
jetzt-wegen-des-preises-buying-chips-on-.text: Frankfurt’s buyers went for the recently battered technology names, Infineon and Siemens Energy among them, wallstreet:online reported [2]. ‘Griffen Anleger am Montag noch wegen der Rückkehr von Jensen Huang zu, kaufen sie jetzt wegen des Preises,’ chief analyst Jochen Stanzl told Handelsblatt [1]. The real question, he said, remains whether the billions invested in AI pay off, especially if rates rise and a growing share is financed on credit [1]. Buying on price is the healthier motive. It means someone did the arithmetic instead of listening to a keynote. This is reporting, not investment advice.

2-trillion-at-the-peak-the-ipo-behind-th.title: $2 trillion at the peak: the IPO behind the free-will row
2-trillion-at-the-peak-the-ipo-behind-th.dek: Anthropic's listing last week was the largest on record.
2-trillion-at-the-peak-the-ipo-behind-th.text: Anthropic’s initial public offering last week was the largest on record, with the company’s value at one point above $2 trillion, Euronews reported [1]. Meta’s AI chief Alexandr Wang warned on Sunday: ‘We should not be okay with a “handover” of society to AI’ [1]. When a company is worth that much, its chief’s philosophy becomes a market fact. That is one more reason for the dull machinery of disclosure.

one-target-met-five-behind-europe-s-anti.title: One target met, five behind: Europe's antibiotic midpoint
one-target-met-five-behind-europe-s-anti.dek: The OECD and the Commission find MRSA bloodstream infections already at the 2030 goal, and a resistant Klebsiella up 72% since 2019. The fix is mostly hand hygiene and prescribing.
one-target-met-five-behind-europe-s-anti.text: Health at a Glance: Europe 2026 takes stock halfway to the EU’s 2030 targets on antimicrobial resistance [1]. One of six is already met: the incidence of MRSA bloodstream infections [1]. Elsewhere the picture is worse. The estimated incidence of bloodstream infections with carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae was 72% higher in 2025 than in 2019, and resistant E. coli infections were also above their 2019 level [1]. Human antibiotic use fell 5% between 2019 and 2025, from 19.9 to 18.9 daily doses per 1,000 people; to reach the target the EU would need a further 16% cut [1]. Austria and Finland have already met their national goals [1]. In animals, veterinary antimicrobial sales fell 24% between 2018 and 2024 [1]. ECDC estimates resistant infections cause more than 35,000 deaths a year in the EU/EEA [1]. The OECD’s modelling says packages of stewardship, better hand hygiene, delayed prescribing and safer food handling save lives and cost less than they save [1]. It is the least glamorous medicine there is. It is also the one that pays for itself. This is reporting, not medical advice.

592-to-35-europe-votes-to-make-its-own-m.title: 592 to 35: Europe votes to make its own medicines
592-to-35-europe-votes-to-make-its-own-m.dek: The Parliament approved the Critical Medicines Act on Wednesday. It rewards local production and allows joint buying.
592-to-35-europe-votes-to-make-its-own-m.text: MEPs in Strasbourg approved the Critical Medicines Act by 592 votes to 35, with 30 abstentions, Agence Europe reported [1]. It sets criteria for projects that can receive national or EU support to build or modernise drug production in the EU; supported firms must prioritise supplies to the European market [1]. Public tenders will reward suppliers in proportion to the share of medicines and active ingredients made in the EU, and at least five member states can launch joint procurement [1]. Shortages are solved in factories and tenders, not in press releases. This law works on both.

35-000-deaths-and-11-7-billion-a-year-th.title: 35,000 deaths and €11.7 billion a year: the price of resistance
35-000-deaths-and-11-7-billion-a-year-th.dek: The OECD counts what resistant infections cost Europe.
35-000-deaths-and-11-7-billion-a-year-th.text: ECDC estimates that infections with antibiotic-resistant bacteria cause more than 35,000 deaths a year in the EU/EEA, the OECD and Commission report notes [1]. OECD modelling puts the combined cost of resistance, from health spending to lost work, at an average of 11.7 billion euros (in purchasing-power terms) a year across the EU to 2050 [1]. Its policy packages, it says, generate savings that exceed their costs [1]. Prevention rarely gets a ribbon-cutting. It gets a smaller bill.

113-drones-87-down-and-250-bodies-home-t.title: 113 drones, 87 down, and 250 bodies home: Thursday's war ledger
113-drones-87-down-and-250-bodies-home-t.dek: Russia struck Kharkiv and Kyiv overnight; Ukraine hit a chemical plant and refineries deep inside Russia. Through the Red Cross, the dead went home.
113-drones-87-down-and-250-bodies-home-t.text: Russia attacked overnight with Iskander-M, Zircon and S-400 missiles and 113 drones, including decoys; Ukraine’s air defences shot down or neutralised 87 targets, Euronews reported [1]. At least three people were killed in Kharkiv, where a residential building and an educational institution were hit, and seven were injured in Kyiv [1]. Ukrainian drones struck the Nevinnomyssky Azot chemical plant in Stavropol region, which produces components for the explosives octogen and hexogen, and the power station beside it; two people were wounded [1]. A new fire broke out at the Kuibyshev refinery in Samara, and the Subkhankulovo pipeline station in Bashkortostan was hit [1]. Russia’s defence ministry claimed 343 Ukrainian drones destroyed; Euronews could not verify that [1]. Through the International Committee of the Red Cross, Russia returned the bodies of 250 servicemen to Ukraine and received 22, according to Russian sources partially confirmed by a Russian search organisation [1]. Zelenskyy warned that Russia is preparing a ‘new massive strike’ on energy facilities [2]. The war’s arithmetic is grim, but the repatriations show one mechanism still functions on a schedule.

pull-back-all-military-aggression-trump-.title: 'Pull back all military aggression': Trump's new sentence
pull-back-all-military-aggression-trump-.dek: After meeting Nato's chief, the US president described what he asked of Putin.
pull-back-all-military-aggression-trump-.text: After talks with Nato secretary general Mark Rutte, Donald Trump wrote that in his discussions with Vladimir Putin in China he had ‘spent a lot of time talking about the fact that I would like to see president Putin pull back all military aggression against territories throughout Europe’, The Guardian reported [1]. What ‘territories throughout Europe’ means was left undefined, the blog noted, after incidents involving Russia in Estonia, Denmark and Poland [1]. A sentence is not a policy. The test is what follows it.

the-conflict-should-not-spread-berlin-on.title: 'The conflict should not spread': Berlin on the Libya strike
the-conflict-should-not-spread-berlin-on.dek: Germany's foreign minister backs Ukraine's self-defence and warns against widening the war.
the-conflict-should-not-spread-berlin-on.text: Commenting on Ukraine’s attack on Russian ships in Libya, Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said Germany supports Ukraine and its right to self-defence, but ‘I strongly warn against allowing this conflict to spread geographically’, France 24 reported, citing Reuters [1]. He spoke at a press conference in Berlin with his Romanian counterpart [1]. Support and restraint in the same sentence is not a contradiction. It is the job description of an ally.

7-000-tonnes-of-diesel-25-miles-from-ibi.title: 7,000 tonnes of diesel, 25 miles from Ibiza: a sheen, not yet a slick
7-000-tonnes-of-diesel-25-miles-from-ibi.dek: A Malta-flagged tanker capsized overnight off a Unesco-listed seabed. One crewman died; the pollution response is running. The difference from 2002 is the cargo and the procedure.
7-000-tonnes-of-diesel-25-miles-from-ibi.text: The Med Emre, a Malta-flagged chemical tanker carrying up to 7,000 tonnes of diesel from Algeciras to Barcelona, capsized 25 nautical miles off Ibiza on Wednesday night [1]. All 17 crew were rescued; seven went to hospital and one later died [1]. The crew had reported a leak and a 90-degree list minutes after a distress call around 22:30 local time [1]. The hull has not sunk completely, which the Balearic emergencies director Pablo Gárriz said makes operations possible at the surface rather than at a depth of 1,000 metres [1]. A plane and Spain’s pollution-control vessel Clara Campoamor are assessing possible damage; ‘there is still little information available about a possible fuel spill’, the Balearic president Marga Prohens wrote [1]. The stakes are real. Ibiza’s marine environment, with its Posidonia seagrass meadows, has been on Unesco’s World Heritage List since 1999 [1]. In 2002 the Prestige spilled more than 60,000 tonnes of heavy fuel oil off Galicia [1]. This time the response began within hours. That is not luck. It is two decades of procedure.

1-to-3-cm-in-eastern-saxony-friday-s-fro.title: 1 to 3 cm in eastern Saxony: Friday's frost map
1-to-3-cm-in-eastern-saxony-friday-s-fro.dek: Snow eased at the Alpine edge on Thursday evening. The east gets a light dusting overnight.
1-to-3-cm-in-eastern-saxony-friday-s-fro.text: High pressure and cold air dominate, with the remnants of an Italian low bringing snow to the south-east, the German weather service said [1]. Thursday brought 3 to 10 cm at the Alpine edge, up to 15 cm in places, easing by evening [1]. Overnight, light snow is expected from Saxony to southern Brandenburg and Thuringia, often little, 1 to 3 cm in eastern Saxony; there is light to moderate frost widely, and persistent frost in the east and south on Friday [1]. Black ice from re-freezing is possible in places [1]. Leave five minutes earlier; the gritting lorries have a schedule too.

58-million-tonnes-the-climate-cost-of-a-.title: 58 million tonnes: the climate cost of a full cupboard
58-million-tonnes-the-climate-cost-of-a-.dek: Stockpiling can turn into waste, and waste into emissions.
58-million-tonnes-the-climate-cost-of-a-.text: Food waste already accounts for up to 10% of global emissions, and food loss and waste generate nearly five times the emissions of aviation, Euronews reports [1]. The EU generated nearly 58 million tonnes of food waste in 2024, more than half from households [1]. Experts quoted warn that excessive stockpiling adds waste, shortages and price rises [1]. The most effective climate measure in many kitchens is a pen and a date on a tin.
